title: Columnar pipelines and schema contracts

objectives.text: Filter and derive columns using one shared row selection while preserving identity and units.
Reject inconsistent column lengths, types and keys before a transform silently truncates or misaligns records.

blocks.markdown: A row-oriented logical record keeps fields together: {trade_id, price_cents, qty}. A column-oriented logical batch groups values by field, with one shared row position across columns. Scanning a few columns can avoid unrelated fields in a true columnar engine, but a Python dictionary of lists is only a teaching representation here. It is not Apache Arrow memory layout and is not a measured performance improvement. Arrow specifies typed buffers and validity metadata; its optimised execution requires an appropriate implementation, not just this container name.

Our input schema has exactly trade_id, price_cents and qty columns, each a list of the same length. IDs are nonempty unique strings. Both numeric columns contain exact nonnegative Python integers excluding bool; they use cents and shares. An empty batch is allowed. This is a strict synthetic contract, not a claim that every real feed uses unique trade rows or disallows corrections. Validate before deriving output, and leave input lists unchanged.

blocks.caption: Expected output: 3, then ['T1', 'T3'], then [200, 900], then 1100. Every selected column uses the same positions. A new notional column is derived only after input validation. The result is a new mapping and lists; scalar field values are immutable.

blocks.markdown: The selection is a list of row positions passing qty > 0. Applying that same selection to every field preserves correspondence. Filtering is a deliberate modeling choice that removes valid zero-quantity rows from this output, not a statement that those source rows were invalid. Record rows read, rows selected and the filter predicate separately from validation rejects. The source count 3 and selected count 2 reconcile to one deliberately filtered row, not one invalid row.

blocks.source:
price_cents = [100, 200]
qty = [3, 1]
print(sum(p * q for p, q in zip(price_cents, qty)))
# This changes only quantity order, breaking the shared row identity.
wrong_qty = sorted(qty)
print(sum(p * q for p, q in zip(price_cents, wrong_qty)))
blocks.caption: Expected output: 500, then 700. Sorting only qty loses which quantity belongs to which price, despite equal lengths and valid numeric types. Sort complete records or apply one common row permutation to all columns. Do not call the changed total a market gain.

blocks.markdown: zip stops when its shortest input ends. Without an equal-length precondition, a price column of length 3 and a quantity column of length 2 can silently produce two derived values. A schema check must run first. Column names, types, null policy, units, identity, ordering and version are separate parts of the contract. A type-valid dataset can still be semantically wrong if units or identities drift.

Adding a column or changing a unit is an interface change. Say which schema versions a consumer accepts, how optional/missing fields are handled and whether an old payload can be migrated without information loss. Do not silently reinterpret a field called price as cents today and dollars tomorrow. Preserve a source identity/revision and transformation description with output so a later discrepancy can be traced.

Independent transfer: copy this synthetic batch, add a new record and predict the selected notional result. Test empty columns, one mismatched length, a duplicate ID, bool in qty and an unexpected extra column. Verify each invalid case raises before returning an output. Snapshot the input before execution and compare afterward to check it was not changed. Then deliberately sort only one column and explain why a schema type check alone cannot catch that semantic bug.

Technical references: [Arrow columnar format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html) for real typed arrays, buffers and validity metadata; [Python zip](https://docs.python.org/3.12/library/functions.html#zip) for shortest-input truncation and the explicit strict mode. This lesson's dictionary-of-lists code demonstrates its own logical alignment and schema contracts only; it does not implement or benchmark Arrow. Filter policy, row identity and arithmetic examples are declared teaching contracts and arguments here, not rules supplied by the Arrow format.

summary: Columns need one shared row identity. Validate lengths/types/keys before deriving values, apply one common selection/permutation, and keep filter counts separate from invalid-input counts. Logical column containers are not automatically an optimised columnar engine.
